title: Torsion vs. Extension Springs: Why Cycle Rating Beats Price
description: Torsion or extension springs — what's actually different, why two 'spring replacement' quotes can vary so much, and why cycle rating matters more than the sticker price.
imageAlt: White garage door with decorative window inserts on a brick home
keywords: torsion spring vs extension spring, garage door spring types, garage door spring cycle rating, garage door spring replacement cost, which garage door spring do I have
h1: Torsion vs. Extension Springs: Why Cycle Rating Beats Price
intro: Call three companies for a spring replacement quote and you can get three different numbers for what sounds like the same job. Part of that is normal shopping-around variance, but part of it is that "spring replacement" isn't one part — it's two different spring systems, several build qualities within each, and a durability spec that most homeowners never hear mentioned. Here's what actually distinguishes torsion from extension springs, and why the cheapest quote on paper is sometimes the most expensive one over ten years.

sections.heading: Two systems, same job: counterbalancing the door
sections.body: Neither spring type lifts the door directly — that's the opener's job, and a modest one at that. What the springs do is counterbalance the door's weight so the opener only has to overcome friction, not hundreds of pounds of steel. Wind either spring type up when the door is down, and it stores the energy to help lift the door back up on the next cycle. The difference is entirely in how that energy gets stored and released, and that difference matters more than most homeowners realize when it's time to replace them.

sections.heading: Torsion springs: the horizontal bar above the door
sections.body:
A torsion spring (or pair of them) sits on a metal shaft mounted horizontally above the closed door, centered over the opening. As the door closes, cables winding onto drums at each end of the shaft twist the spring tighter, storing energy in torque rather than stretch. That torque unwinds through the drums and cables to lift the door evenly from both sides.

This is the standard on most garage doors built or updated in the last couple of decades, and for good reason: torsion springs distribute lifting force evenly across the door, last longer under the same duty because the stress is spread more efficiently through the coil, and — critically — fail in a more contained way. When a torsion spring lets go, it's still mounted on its shaft; it doesn't become a projectile the way an unrestrained extension spring can.

sections.heading: Extension springs: stretched along the horizontal tracks
sections.body:
Extension springs run along the horizontal tracks on either side of the door, stretching as the door closes and pulling back to help lift it open. They're common on older installations and lower-cost door systems, largely because the hardware is cheaper to manufacture and install.

The tradeoff is safety and longevity. An extension spring under full tension that snaps can whip violently along the track — which is exactly why modern code requires a **safety cable** threaded through the center of every extension spring, so a failure is contained instead of launching a broken spring or its end hook across the garage. If your door has extension springs without visible safety cables running through them, that's worth flagging on your next service visit regardless of whether anything else seems wrong.

sections.heading: Why cycle rating matters more than the sticker price
sections.body:
Every spring — torsion or extension — has a rated lifespan measured in cycles, not years. One cycle is one full open-and-close. A standard-grade spring is typically rated around 10,000 cycles, which sounds like a lot until you count: a door cycling 4 times a day burns through that in about 7 years, which is why a spring quietly "just breaks" around the same age on so many houses.

Here's the part that doesn't show up on a quick phone quote: two springs can look identical and cost the same to install, but be built from noticeably different-gauge steel with very different real-world cycle life. A heavier-gauge, higher-cycle spring costs modestly more in material and lasts proportionally longer — often years longer — for a small difference in the total bill. When a quote is unusually cheap, ask what cycle rating the spring is built to; that answer tells you more about long-term value than the price alone does.

sections.heading: What replacement costs, and why we quote it upfront
sections.body:
Spring replacement in our service area generally runs **$175 to $350**, depending on whether it's a torsion or extension system, single or double-spring, and door size and weight. We give the exact price before any work begins — no guessing on the phone and no surprise number once a technician is standing in the garage.

One rule we don't bend on regardless of spring type: **replace both springs on a two-spring door.** Both springs wind the same number of cycles over their life, so when one fails, the other is at the same fatigue point and is typically only months from following it. Replacing just the broken one is a false economy that tends to mean a second service call within the year.

sections.heading: Why this is never a DIY repair
sections.body: Whichever type your door has, the spring is storing enough force to lift a 150-plus-pound door several feet in the air — and releasing that energy in an uncontrolled way is how garage door spring injuries happen every year. Professionals use winding bars and clamps rated for the job, unwind or wind the spring in a controlled sequence, and finish with a balance test: the door should stay put at roughly half-height without drifting up or down. That balance test is the real proof the job was done correctly, on either spring type, and it's the step DIY attempts almost always skip.

faq.question: How do I know if my garage door has torsion or extension springs?
faq.answer: Look above the closed door. A torsion spring is a single tightly-wound coil mounted on a horizontal metal bar centered over the door opening. Extension springs are long, thinner coils that run along the horizontal tracks on the sides of the door, above the rollers, and stretch as the door closes.

faq.question: Are torsion springs better than extension springs?
faq.answer: For most homes, yes. Torsion springs distribute the door's weight more evenly, generally last longer under the same duty cycle, and fail in a more contained way since the spring stays mounted on its shaft. Extension springs are still safe when properly installed with a safety cable through the coil, but if yours lack that cable, it's worth having a technician check on the next visit.

faq.question: What does garage door spring replacement cost?
faq.answer: Generally $175 to $350 in our service area, depending on spring type, whether it's a single or double-spring system, and the door's size and weight. We give the exact price before starting any work, and it's normally a same-visit repair.

faq.question: Should I replace one spring or both if only one broke?
faq.answer: Both, on a two-spring door. Both springs have wound the same number of cycles and are at essentially the same point in their fatigue life, so the surviving spring is likely to fail within months of the first. Replacing them as a pair in one visit avoids paying for a second service call soon after.
